result.markdown: # Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions {#i-ep02 .unnumbered} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 2, you can - fit and interpret a multiple regression with dummies, interactions, and curves, - compare nested models and test groups of terms with a partial F-test, - read a regression table from a research paper and state its limits, - check an AI answer about a regression and use a confidence interval for a decision. ::: Tutorials are exam preparation sessions. The tasks below are exam-style questions. Try each task yourself before you look at the solution. You may use AI for this, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 4 and 5. Lecture 6 is on the day before this tutorial: read its lecture material, and do its practice after the tutorial. Use the complete [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) while working. If needed, review [Mathematics Refresher: indicators and reference categories](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#indicators-and-reference-categories), [products, interactions, and combined effects](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#products-interactions-and-combined-effects), and [polynomial terms](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#polynomial-terms). Complete from memory: 1. You interpret a multiple-regression slope while ... 2. A dummy coefficient compares ... 3. An interaction coefficient is a difference in ... 4. A partial F-test compares ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. Holding the other included predictors fixed. 2. A category with the named reference category. 3. Slopes. 4. A reduced nested model with a complete model on the same observations. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial Try each task in R before you open the answer. More practice for home is in the final section of this page, [Extra practice for home](#i-ep02-home). Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of dollars. Tutorial 1 asked how a single predictor relates to the outcome. This tutorial asks what changes when several predictors are held fixed at the same time, when categories enter the model, and when a slope depends on a group or on the season. First build the data for the analysis, with the same steps as in Lectures 4 to 6. The code converts the requested amount to thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). It keeps the 874 deals for a share of the company (`deals`) for Task 1. For Tasks 2 to 4 it keeps the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`). The 7 pitches with an unknown team are left out, so that all models of Tasks 2 to 4 use the same observations. Then it makes all-men teams the reference category of the team variable, builds the dummy `women` (1 for all-women and mixed teams), and centres the season at its mean. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group), ref = "all_men") known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) ``` ::: ### Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} How much of the company do founders give up in a deal, once the season and the size of the request are taken into account? With the 874 deals for a share of the company (`deals`), fit a regression of the equity agreed in the deal, in percent (`deal_equity_pct`), on the equity that the founder first offered, in percent (`equity_offered_pct`), the season (`season`), and the requested amount in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). Then answer these questions. 1. Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are held fixed, in one sentence each. 2. The simple regression of the agreed equity on the equity offered, with the same deals, gives a slope of about 1.21. Compare it with the slope of the equity offered in your model, and explain in one or two sentences why the slope changed. 3. Interpret $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ in one sentence each. Then name the two models that the overall F-test compares, and state its conclusion at the 5% level. 4. Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects, in one sentence each. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Interpretation of the equity-offered slope: Interpretation of the season slope: Interpretation of the requested-amount slope: Change in the equity-offered slope, and why: R-squared: Adjusted R-squared: Overall F-test, the two models it compares, and its conclusion: Two reasons why the coefficients are not causal effects: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lm( deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct + season + ask_1k, data = deals ) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct + season + ask_1k, data = deals) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -36.313 -6.296 -1.404 3.789 84.040 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 17.762075 1.450891 12.242 < 2e-16 *** equity_offered_pct 1.043787 0.053896 19.367 < 2e-16 *** season -0.625606 0.098959 -6.322 4.13e-10 *** ask_1k -0.005101 0.001268 -4.024 6.23e-05 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 11.15 on 870 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.4327, Adjusted R-squared: 0.4307 F-statistic: 221.1 on 3 and 870 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(deals$deal_equity_pct) # benchmark: mean agreed equity ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 23.55902 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cor(deals$season, deals[, c("equity_offered_pct", "deal_equity_pct")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` equity_offered_pct deal_equity_pct [1,] -0.3995938 -0.4005848 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Interpretation of the equity-offered slope: among the 874 deals, at the same season and requested amount, a founder who offers one percentage point more gives up on average about 1.04 percentage points more in the deal. - Interpretation of the season slope: at the same offer and requested amount, one later season is associated with about 0.63 percentage points less agreed equity, on average. Over ten seasons this adds up to about 6.3 points, about a quarter of the mean agreed share of 23.6%. - Interpretation of the requested-amount slope: at the same offer and season, an extra \$1,000 requested is associated with about 0.0051 percentage points less agreed equity (about 0.51 points per \$100,000), on average. - Change in the equity-offered slope, and why: the slope falls from about 1.21 to about 1.04. In early seasons founders offered larger shares and the sharks also took larger shares (both correlations with the season are about $-0.40$), so the simple slope partly picked up this season pattern, and holding the season fixed removes that part. - R-squared: $R^2\approx0.433$, so the three predictors explain about 43% of the variation in the agreed equity among these deals. - Adjusted R-squared: $0.431$, almost the same, because the penalty for three predictors is small with 874 deals. - Overall F-test, the two models it compares, and its conclusion: it compares the model with the intercept-only model. It gives $F\approx221.1$ on 3 and 870 degrees of freedom, with a p-value below 0.001, so it rejects the null hypothesis that all three slopes are zero. - Two reasons why the coefficients are not causal effects: any two of these. Only pitches that ended in a deal on air are in the data. The quality of the venture is not measured, and it can affect both the share that a founder offers and the share that the sharks take. The amounts and shares may be measured with error. ::: ### Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Do founders in some industries offer a different share of their company? Use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`). Fit a reduced model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`). Fit a complete model that adds the industry of the venture (`industry`, 16 industries), with Food and Beverage, the largest industry, as the reference category. 1. Say how many dummy coefficients the complete model has, and explain in one sentence why. 2. Interpret the coefficient of Technology/Software in one sentence. Judge its size in one sentence, as a percent of the mean equity offered in these pitches. 3. Test with a partial F-test at the 5% level, with the p-value approach, whether all industry coefficients are jointly zero. 4. The t-test of the Technology/Software coefficient and the partial F-test lead to different conclusions. Explain in one or two sentences how this can happen. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Number of dummy coefficients, and why: Interpretation of the Technology/Software coefficient: Size, as a percent of the mean equity offered: Null hypothesis H0: and alternative hypothesis H1: Test statistic formula: Values in the formula: Value of the test statistic: P-value: Conclusion: Why the t-test and the F-test can disagree: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} known_gender$industry <- relevel(factor(known_gender$industry), ref = "Food and Beverage") reduced <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + industry, data = known_gender) summary(complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + industry, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.244 -4.820 -1.218 3.311 82.151 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 21.2651814 0.6310639 33.697 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8185659 0.0479217 -17.081 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028289 0.0005913 -4.784 1.9e-06 *** industryAutomotive -2.4430406 1.8953084 -1.289 0.19761 industryBusiness Services -0.9348173 1.2512415 -0.747 0.45512 industryChildren/Education -0.6722195 0.7946090 -0.846 0.39771 industryElectronics 2.1240268 1.8466736 1.150 0.25026 industryFashion/Beauty 0.3419339 0.6618942 0.517 0.60552 industryFitness/Sports/Outdoors 0.6969671 0.7643920 0.912 0.36203 industryGreen/CleanTech -0.8773490 2.0808047 -0.422 0.67335 industryHealth/Wellness -0.6509551 1.0259488 -0.634 0.52586 industryLifestyle/Home 0.3073560 0.6466161 0.475 0.63463 industryLiquor/Alcohol -3.6604943 2.3345915 -1.568 0.11712 industryMedia/Entertainment -0.5257577 1.5137331 -0.347 0.72840 industryPet Products 0.7576323 1.0750654 0.705 0.48109 industryTechnology/Software -2.9450726 1.0143925 -2.903 0.00375 ** industryTravel 3.4591759 2.3500586 1.472 0.14126 industryUncertain/Other 0.8209125 1.6465742 0.499 0.61817 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.603 on 1416 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.2004, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1908 F-statistic: 20.88 on 17 and 1416 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(reduced, complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + industry Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1431 83228 2 1416 81858 15 1370.6 1.5806 0.07183 . --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(known_gender$equity_offered_pct) # benchmark: mean equity offered ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 13.21978 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Number of dummy coefficients, and why: 15, one for each of the 16 industries except the reference category Food and Beverage. - Interpretation of the Technology/Software coefficient: at the same season and requested amount, Technology/Software pitches are fitted to offer about 2.95 percentage points less equity than Food and Beverage pitches (p $\approx$ 0.004). - Size, as a percent of the mean equity offered: 2.95 points is about 22% of the mean equity offered of 13.2%, a sizeable difference for a founder. - Null hypothesis H0: all 15 industry coefficients are zero. Alternative hypothesis H1: at least one of them is not zero. - Test statistic formula: $F=\dfrac{(\text{SSE}_R-\text{SSE}_C)/q}{\text{SSE}_C/(n-k_C-1)}$. - Values in the formula: $\text{SSE}_R=83{,}228$, $\text{SSE}_C=81{,}858$, $q=15$, and $n-k_C-1=1{,}434-17-1=1{,}416$. - Value of the test statistic: $F=\dfrac{1{,}370.6/15}{81{,}858/1{,}416}=\dfrac{91.37}{57.81}\approx1.58$. - P-value: about 0.072. - Conclusion: since $0.072>0.05$, do not reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The data do not show that the industry terms together improve the model. This does not prove that all industries offer the same share. - Why the t-test and the F-test can disagree: the F-test asks whether the 15 industry terms together improve the model, while each t-test asks about one comparison with Food and Beverage. With 15 separate t-tests at the 5% level, one p-value below 0.05 can easily occur by chance even if no industry differs, because each test rejects a true null hypothesis in about 1 of 20 cases. ::: ### Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`), fit a regression of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the centred season `season_c`, the dummy `women` (1 for all-women and mixed teams), their interaction, and the requested amount (`ask_1k`). 1. Write the fitted line for `women = 0` and for `women = 1` at a requested amount of \$100,000. Give both season slopes. 2. Calculate the fitted difference in the equity offered between a team with women and an all-men team in Season 4, at the same requested amount. 3. Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value in one or two sentences, without claiming too much in either direction. 4. Explain in one or two sentences what centring the season changes and what it does not change. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Fitted line for women = 0: Fitted line for women = 1: Season slope for all-men teams: Season slope for teams with women: Fitted difference in Season 4: Interpretation of the interaction estimate and its p-value: What centring changes and what it does not change: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_interaction <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(m_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.871 -4.742 -1.290 3.412 82.689 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 13.6247907 0.3354522 40.616 < 2e-16 *** season_c -0.7993817 0.0663226 -12.053 < 2e-16 *** women 0.8069665 0.4117061 1.960 0.0502 . ask_1k -0.0026776 0.0005834 -4.590 4.83e-06 *** season_c:women -0.0614594 0.0955667 -0.643 0.5203 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.62 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1894, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1871 F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(known_gender$season) # average season, used for centring ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8.77894 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Fitted line for women = 0: the intercept at \$100,000 requested is $13.625-0.00268\times100\approx13.357$, so the line is $13.357-0.799\,\text{season\_c}$. - Fitted line for women = 1: the intercept is $13.357+0.807=14.164$, so the line is $14.164-0.861\,\text{season\_c}$. - Season slope for all-men teams: about $-0.799$ percentage points per season. - Season slope for teams with women: $-0.7994-0.0615\approx-0.861$ percentage points per season. - Fitted difference in Season 4: the average season is about 8.78, so Season 4 is $\text{season\_c}=4-8.78=-4.78$. The difference is $0.807+(-0.0615)\times(-4.78)\approx1.10$ percentage points, about 8% of the mean equity offered of 13.2%. - Interpretation of the interaction estimate and its p-value: the estimated difference in slopes is $-0.061$ percentage points per season, with p $\approx$ 0.520, so the model gives no evidence that the season trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise. - What centring changes and what it does not change: centring makes the `women` coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8) and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate. ::: ### Task 4: Polynomial term (Lecture 6) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`), fit a linear model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`), and a quadratic model that adds the square of the season. 1. Decide with a partial F-test at the 5% level whether the quadratic term improves the model. 2. Calculate the fitted change from Season 2 to Season 3 and from Season 14 to Season 15, at the same requested amount. Say in one sentence what the comparison of the two changes shows. 3. Calculate the fitted change from Season 18 to Season 19. Explain in one or two sentences why you should not use this number. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Null hypothesis H0: and alternative hypothesis H1: Value of the test statistic: P-value: Conclusion: Fitted change from Season 2 to Season 3: Fitted change from Season 14 to Season 15: What the comparison shows: Fitted change from Season 18 to Season 19: Why not to use this number: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) m_quadratic <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.160 -4.540 -1.010 3.401 82.003 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.1677366 0.8217246 29.411 < 2e-16 *** season -1.7128060 0.2059832 -8.315 < 2e-16 *** I(season^2) 0.0509421 0.0113830 4.475 8.24e-06 *** ask_1k -0.0026921 0.0005749 -4.682 3.10e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.576 on 1430 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1982, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1966 F-statistic: 117.9 on 3 and 1430 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_linear, m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1431 83228 2 1430 82079 1 1149.6 20.028 8.236e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} b <- coef(m_quadratic) # fitted change from season x to x + 1, for x = 2, 14, and 18 b["season"] + b["I(season^2)"] * (2 * c(2, 14, 18) + 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -1.4580954 -0.2354846 0.1720523 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Null hypothesis H0: the coefficient of the quadratic term is zero. Alternative hypothesis H1: it is not zero. - Value of the test statistic: $F\approx20.0$, on 1 and 1,430 degrees of freedom. - P-value: below 0.001. - Conclusion: reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The quadratic term improves the model. - Fitted change from Season 2 to Season 3: with $\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713$ and $\hat\beta_2\approx0.0509$, the change is $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times2+1)=-1.713+5\times0.0509\approx-1.46$ percentage points, about 11% of the mean equity offered of 13.2%. - Fitted change from Season 14 to Season 15: $-1.713+29\times0.0509\approx-0.24$ percentage points. - What the comparison shows: the fitted decline flattens, from about 1.5 points per season in the early seasons to less than a quarter point per season in the late seasons. - Fitted change from Season 18 to Season 19: $-1.713+37\times0.0509\approx+0.17$ percentage points, a rise. - Why not to use this number: the data contain no season after 16, so nothing in the data supports this rise. A quadratic curve always turns somewhere, and the rise only follows from that shape. ::: ### The models of Tasks 2 to 4 in one table {#iep02-spec-table} [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 4 showed how research papers put several models side by side in one regression table. The table below does this for the models of Tasks 2 to 4. All columns of such a table must use the same observations. Tasks 2 to 4 all use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`), so their models fit in one table. The code prints the one model output that the answers above do not show, the reduced model of Task 2. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(reduced) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.169 -4.814 -1.136 3.277 82.219 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 21.1849717 0.4838230 43.787 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8152726 0.0472948 -17.238 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028517 0.0005776 -4.937 8.87e-07 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.626 on 1431 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.187, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1859 F-statistic: 164.6 on 2 and 1431 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Column (1) is the reduced model of Task 2 (`reduced`), column (2) the complete model of Task 2 (`complete`), column (3) the interaction model of Task 3 (`m_interaction`), and column (4) the quadratic model of Task 4 (`m_quadratic`). ::: {.reg-table} | | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) | |:---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Season | −0.815\*\*\* | −0.819\*\*\* | −0.799\*\*\* | −1.713\*\*\* | | | (0.047) | (0.048) | (0.066) | (0.206) | | Season squared | | | | 0.051\*\*\* | | | | | | (0.011) | | Amount requested (\$1,000s) | −0.0029\*\*\* | −0.0028\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | | | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | | Industry dummies (15) | | Yes | | | | Team with women (all-women or mixed) | | | 0.807 | | | | | | (0.412) | | | Season × team with women | | | −0.061 | | | | | | (0.096) | | | Intercept | 21.185\*\*\* | 21.265\*\*\* | 13.625\*\*\* | 24.168\*\*\* | | | (0.484) | (0.631) | (0.335) | (0.822) | | Observations | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | | $R^2$ | 0.187 | 0.200 | 0.189 | 0.198 | | Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.186 | 0.191 | 0.187 | 0.197 | ::: Outcome: equity offered (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. All four columns use the same 1,434 pitches with a known team classification. In column (2), "Yes" means that the model contains the 15 industry dummies, with Food and Beverage as the reference category. Many papers report a large set of dummies in this short way. In column (3) the reference category is all-men teams, and season is centred at its mean (about 8.8), so the intercept and the coefficient of "Team with women" refer to the average season. \* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001. Read along the Season row. The coefficient is close to $-0.8$ in columns (1) to (3). In column (4) it is $-1.713$, because with the quadratic term in the model the season coefficient alone is not the trend. Read down a column to see one model. Columns (2), (3), and (4) each add terms to column (1), so a partial F-test can compare each of them with column (1). The bottom rows show that the four models fit almost equally well: adjusted $R^2$ lies between 0.186 and 0.197, a difference of about one percentage point of the variation in the equity offered. Use this layout for regression results in your thesis. ### Task 5: Read a regression table from a paper The table below has the layout of a regression table in a research paper, the same layout as the table above. The outcome is entrepreneurial intention on a scale from 1 to 7, measured in a survey of 265 students. Self-efficacy is a score from 1 to 7 for how confident a student is that he or she can start a business. The table does not show the intercept. Some journals do this. ::: {.reg-table} | | (1) | (2) | |:---|---:|---:| | Age (years) | 0.02 | 0.01 | | | (0.02) | (0.02) | | Female (1 = yes) | −0.21\* | −0.15 | | | (0.10) | (0.10) | | Prior entrepreneurial experience (1 = yes) | | 0.42\*\* | | | | (0.13) | | Entrepreneurial self-efficacy (1--7) | | 0.38\*\*\* | | | | (0.07) | | Observations | 265 | 265 | | $R^2$ | 0.03 | 0.19 | | Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.02 | 0.18 | ::: Outcome: entrepreneurial intention (scale from 1 to 7). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. \* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001. 1. Say in one sentence each what the numbers in parentheses and the stars mean. Then check the stars of the self-efficacy coefficient with its t statistic. The critical value is $t_{0.975,\,260}=1.969$. 2. The coefficient of Female changes from $-0.21$ with a star in column (1) to $-0.15$ without a star in column (2). Explain in one or two sentences why the coefficient changed. Then say in one or two sentences what the missing star does and does not mean. 3. $R^2$ rises from 0.03 to 0.19. Say in one sentence what that means, and name the test that shows whether the two added predictors are jointly significant. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text Numbers in parentheses: Stars: t statistic of self-efficacy, and check of its stars: What happened to the Female coefficient: What the missing star does and does not mean: What the rise in R-squared says: Test of the two added predictors: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Filled-in structure: - Numbers in parentheses: the standard errors of the coefficients. - Stars: the p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against zero, with more stars for a smaller p-value. - t statistic of self-efficacy, and check of its stars: $t_{obs}=0.38/0.07\approx5.4$. This is far beyond the critical value $t_{0.975,\,260}$ = `qt(0.975, 260)` = 1.969, and p is below 0.001, so three stars are correct. - What happened to the Female coefficient: model (2) holds experience and self-efficacy fixed as well, so the coefficient now compares women and men with the same age, experience, and self-efficacy. Part of the difference of 0.21 points in column (1) went together with differences in experience and self-efficacy. - What the missing star does and does not mean: the 95% confidence interval around $-0.15$ includes zero. It does not show that the difference is zero. - What the rise in R-squared says: the two added predictors explain a further 16 percentage points of the variation in intentions in this sample. - Test of the two added predictors: a partial F-test of the two nested models, model (1) against model (2) on the same 265 students. If you have the data, `anova()` of the two fitted models gives this test. ::: ### Task 6: A/B test, moderator and mediator (Lectures 5 and 6) (a) An online shop for refurbished phones shows 120 new visitors either its current product page (`new_page = 0`) or a new page with customer videos (`new_page = 1`). Chance decides which page each visitor sees, 60 visitors per page. The outcome is the value of the first order in euros. The code below creates the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(21) # random assignment: 60 zeros (old page) and 60 ones (new page) new_page <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = 60)) # order values in euros, simulated with a true effect of 3 euros order_value <- round(40 + 3 * new_page + rnorm(120, mean = 0, sd = 8), 2) ab_shop <- data.frame(new_page, order_value) ``` ::: Regress `order_value` on the treatment dummy `new_page`. Test in five steps, with the critical value approach at the 5% level, whether the new page changes the mean order value. The critical value is $t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$. Explain in one or two sentences why $\hat\beta_1$ estimates the average treatment effect of the new page. Judge its size as a percent of the mean order value with the old page. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Hypotheses: Test statistic: Critical value and rejection region: Observed value: Conclusion: Why the coefficient estimates the average treatment effect: Size, as a percent of the mean order value with the old page: ``` (b) A meal-kit start-up gives a discount coupon at random to half of its customers. Customers with the coupon order more meal kits. The coupon raises orders more for students than for other customers. The coupon also brings customers to the website more often, and more visits go with more orders. Which variable is a moderator, and which is a mediator? Say in one or two sentences each how it appears in a regression of orders on the coupon dummy. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text Moderator, and how it appears in the regression: Mediator, and how it appears in the regression: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer (a) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ab_fit <- lm(order_value ~ new_page, data = ab_shop) summary(ab_fit)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 39.086333 0.9480553 41.22790 6.427869e-72 new_page 3.409333 1.3407527 2.54285 1.228932e-02 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} qt(0.975, df = 118) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.980272 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Hypotheses: $H_0:\beta_1=0$, the new page has no effect on the mean order value. $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. The significance level is 5%. - Test statistic: $T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, with $df=n-k-1=118$. - Critical value and rejection region: $t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$. Reject $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge1.980$. - Observed value: $t_{obs}=3.409/1.341\approx2.54$. - Conclusion: $2.54\ge1.980$, so reject $H_0$ (p $\approx$ 0.012). At the 5% level, the new page raises the mean order value. - Why the coefficient estimates the average treatment effect: chance decided who saw the new page, so the two groups are alike on average in everything else, measured or not, and the only systematic difference is the page. - Size, as a percent of the mean order value with the old page: the mean order value is 39.09 euros with the old page (the intercept) and $39.09+3.41=42.50$ euros with the new page. The effect of about 3.41 euros is about 8.7% of 39.09 euros. (b) Filled-in structure: - Moderator, and how it appears in the regression: student status is the moderator, because it changes the slope of the coupon. It enters as an interaction, `lm(orders ~ coupon * student)`, and the coefficient of `coupon:student` is the difference in the coupon effect between students and other customers. - Mediator, and how it appears in the regression: website visits are the mediator, because they lie on the path from the coupon to orders. Adding visits, `lm(orders ~ coupon + visits)`, shrinks the coupon coefficient to the direct part, so for the total effect of the coupon, leave visits out of the model. ::: ### Task 7: Check the AI (Lectures 4 to 6) Lisa runs a café on campus. Show the solution only after I send my answer." ::: ## Extra practice for home {#i-ep02-home} This task practises the one-way ANOVA table at home. ### Task 8: A one-way ANOVA (Lecture 5) The online shop for refurbished phones of Task 6 records the delivery time in hours of 20 orders for each of three couriers. The code below creates the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(7) courier <- factor(rep(c("cycle", "post", "van"), each = 20)) delivery_hours <- round(c(rnorm(20, 20, 6), rnorm(20, 26, 6), rnorm(20, 22, 6)), 1) deliveries <- data.frame(courier, delivery_hours) ``` ::: Fit the regression of `delivery_hours` on `courier` and make its ANOVA table. Say which dummies this regression uses, and say in one sentence each what its two dummy coefficients mean. Test in five steps, with the critical value approach at the 5% level, whether the mean delivery time is the same for the three couriers. The critical value of this F-test is 3.16. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Dummies in the regression: Meaning of the two dummy coefficients: Hypotheses: Test statistic, with both degrees of freedom: Critical value and rejection region: Observed value: Conclusion: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} courier_fit <- lm(delivery_hours ~ courier, data = deliveries) coef(courier_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) courierpost couriervan 22.650 3.935 -0.015 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(courier_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: delivery_hours Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) courier 2 207.25 103.623 2.9512 0.06031 . Residuals 57 2001.40 35.112 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(deliveries$delivery_hours) # overall mean ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 23.95667 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} qf(0.95, 2, 57) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.158843 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Dummies in the regression: `post` and `van`, with `cycle` as the reference category. - Meaning of the two dummy coefficients: the intercept, 22.65 hours, is the mean delivery time of the cycle courier. The post courier takes on average 3.94 hours longer, and the van courier 0.02 hours less. - Hypotheses: $H_0:\mu_{\text{cycle}}=\mu_{\text{post}}=\mu_{\text{van}}$. $H_1$: at least one mean differs. The significance level is 5%. - Test statistic, with both degrees of freedom: $F$ = mean square of `courier` divided by the mean square of the residuals, with $G-1=2$ and $n-G=57$ degrees of freedom. - Critical value and rejection region: the critical value is 3.16. Reject $H_0$ if $F_{obs}\ge3.16$. - Observed value: $F_{obs}=103.62/35.11\approx2.95$. - Conclusion: $2.95<3.16$ (p $\approx$ 0.060), so do not reject $H_0$. At the 5% level, the data do not show that the mean delivery time differs between the couriers. This does not prove that the means are equal.
